title: Socioeconomic variations in the course of stroke: unequal health outcomes, equal care?
D1_Risk_Reasoning: The study uses a multicentre cohort from 23 randomly selected hospitals, providing a representative sample of hospitalised stroke patients in the Netherlands. Inclusion/exclusion and baseline characteristics are well-defined.
D1_Source_Evidence: Patients were recruited from admissions to 23 randomly selected hospitals in the Netherlands.
D1_Source_Reasoning: The source population is clearly defined as hospitalised stroke patients across a broad geographic range (23 hospitals).
D1_Method_Evidence: All 760 patients were admitted within one week after stroke onset to 23 randomly selected Dutch hospitals.
D1_Method_Reasoning: Random selection of hospitals and a clear timeframe for admission (within one week) minimize recruitment bias.
D1_Period_Reasoning: While the follow-up duration (5 years) is mentioned, the specific calendar years of recruitment are not explicitly stated in the text.
D1_Place_Evidence: 23 randomly selected hospitals in the Netherlands.
D1_Place_Reasoning: The setting (hospitals) and geographic location (Netherlands) are clearly specified.
D1_Criteria_Evidence: 465 patients were included who had had a stroke six months earlier... analyses necessarily were confined to the six months survivors.
D1_Criteria_Reasoning: The study defines the 'zero time' for this analysis as 6 months post-stroke and specifies the exclusion of those who died before this point.
D1_Participation_Evidence: Of the 502 patients who were still alive after six months, 17 patients refused to participate in the interview and for 20 patients socioeconomic status—that is, educational level—was unknown.
D1_Participation_Reasoning: The participation rate among eligible 6-month survivors is high (465/502 = 92.6%).
D1_Baseline_Evidence: Table 1 describes the characteristics of the patients in the study group by socioeconomic status.
D1_Baseline_Reasoning: Table 1 provides a comprehensive list of age, gender, stroke severity, type, and recurrent stroke status.
D2_Risk_Reasoning: While mortality is high (expected in stroke), the authors explicitly addressed selective mortality by performing sensitivity analyses on 5-year survivors. However, detailed characteristics of non-mortality dropouts are sparse.
D2_Response_Evidence: The cumulative mortality was 34% at six months, 51% at three years, and 62% at five years.
D2_Response_Reasoning: High attrition due to mortality is inherent to the condition, but it significantly reduces the sample size for long-term analysis.
D2_Attempts_Reasoning: The text does not describe specific efforts to trace or collect data on those who refused or were lost for reasons other than death.
D2_Reasons_Evidence: 17 patients refused to participate... 20 patients socioeconomic status... was unknown... cumulative mortality was 34% at six months...

D2_DropoutChar_Reasoning: The paper does not provide a comparison table between those lost to follow-up (non-deaths) and those who completed the study.
D2_Diff_Evidence: The problem of the possible selective effect of socioeconomic status on mortality was tackled by repeating the analyses including only the survivors of five years after stroke.
D2_Diff_Reasoning: The authors acknowledge the potential for bias and attempt to control for it via sensitivity analysis, but do not definitively prove no difference exists for non-mortality dropouts.
D3_Risk_Reasoning: Socioeconomic status (SES) is clearly defined by education level, a standard and stable metric for this age group. Measurement was consistent across the cohort.
